Texas perennial often forming a small to moderate upright tuft from shallow, hard, branched rhizomatous bases.
Fine basal blades; narrower stem blades often only a few mm wide.
Loose/slender, often broken or interrupted spike-like panicle, in local treatment about 5–15 cm long.
Spotted purplish 3–3.6 mm spikelets in local flora treatment; observe mature structures before claiming exact ID.
True ligule can form a hair curtain around 1–2 mm; hairs in the leaf collar can be longer and must not be mistaken for the ligule.

Inspect an intact attached SPIKELET at 10–20×. Count the SUBTENDING PERSISTENT BRISTLES (sterile branches), not grass awns or protruding flower parts.
Record bristle count/length and spikelet length using a 1-mm scale, and compare the same-plant collar ligule.
Check a rooted base only where collecting is legal: annual fibrous millet vs knotty rhizomatous perennial parviflora/reverchonii, and perennial scheelei.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Compared with S. parviflora, Reverchon's bristlegrass has a more interrupted narrow head and much fewer attached bristles (parviflora typically 4–12 per spikelet). S. scheelei has conspicuously long spreading bristles commonly 10–35 mm and a longer tapering head, often broad hairy leaves. Millet S. italica is an annual crop/escape with heavy dense terminal heads. Panicle texture varies with maturity, so verify bristles at the spikelet base.
not_reliable_alone: Color or texture of seedhead without bristle group macro
Bristles mistaken for true floret awns or flower stigmas
Mature spikelet counts read from a photo too small to show attachment
Cultivated or habitat context presented as confirmed local nativity

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.look_here_first: On a perennial with short sometimes knotty rhizomes, trace the narrow, often INTERRUPTED erect panicle and inspect several spikelet bases: sparse bristles can be absent on some portions; when present generally 2–8 mm, not a hard ≤2-mm cutoff.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.measured_growth_and_collar: Perennial with short sometimes knotty rhizomes; culms ~30–90 cm. Narrow blades ~1–7 mm; ligule a 1–2-mm fringe of stiff hairs at actual blade/sheath junction. Sheaths can carry papillose-based hairs; distinguish longer collar hairs from the true ligule fringe.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.measured_inflorescence_and_bristles: Erect slender interrupted panicle ~5–20 cm; scabrous rachis; sparse persistent sterile branchlet bristles, ~2–8 mm where present. Mature spikelets elliptic to obovate ~2.1–4.5 mm. Measure several attachments on a single confirmed plant.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.measured_spikelet_glumes_lemmas_awns: Lower glume approximately 1/2 spikelet length, 5–7-veined; upper glume about as long as upper fertile lemma, 7–9-veined. Lower sterile lemma near fertile lemma length, lower palea absent. Upper fertile lemma firm, finely cross-wrinkled; upper palea similarly firm. Spikelets lack true long glume/lemma awns: do not mistake subtending bristles for awns.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: S. parviflora has short dense even-width heads, 4–12 bristles per spikelet and knotty rhizomes; S. scheelei has a long tapering head and usually single 10–35-mm bristles; introduced S. italica has a heavy dense head and annual fibrous roots. Never identify from interrupted head silhouette alone.
last_mile_photo_holds: Same legally photographed rooted perennial base with short rhizome and complete interrupted head plus centimeter ruler.
Several 10–20× mature spikelet attachments, including truly absent versus present 2–8-mm bristles, with mm scale; no invented arrow on invisible bristle.
Exposed 1–2-mm stiff hair ligule separate from sheath-mouth hairs with mm ruler.
Dissected mature spikelet showing both glumes, sterile lemma and transversely rugose fertile lemma; paired scale-matched S. parviflora and S. scheelei.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.public_ready_criteria: Retain existing Eric Knight CC BY photo, arrows, taxonomy and nativity holds. Keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until actual licensed species-vetted microscopic and collar evidence, pixel-verified arrows, and public page QA.

items.label: Foxtail millet — dense, nodding cultivated seedheads
items.image_role: Real existing garden/crop overview showing branching millet head silhouette rather than microscopic identity
items.caption: Original credited overview shows multiple long densely packed, at times curved and drooping foxtail-millet heads with relatively wide leaves. It cannot expose individual basal bristle counts, ligules, exact millimeters or true annual root system.
items.why_it_matters: FOXTAIL MILLET (INTRODUCED annual crop/escape): start with stout annual culms, broad foliage, and a heavy dense often lobed or nodding foxtail head. Flora of North America usually describes 1–3 persistent subtending bristles (to ~12 mm), NOT 'numerous bristles beneath every spikelet'. A crop-derived head varies greatly; distinguish from perennial native bristlegrasses using rooted duration, panicle shape and ripe spikelets.
items.creator: Dinesh Valke
items.photo_status: Source labelled and locally archived real JPEG visually inspected 2026-10-21. Targets show only gross structures actually visible. Source identity provisional; bristle counts, microscopy and local nativity NOT independently proven.

items.label: Knotroot bristlegrass — reproductive close-up with 2-mm scale
items.image_role: Real original photographed flower detail, not diagnostic complete seedhead or rooted plant
items.caption: Original Stefan.lefnaer macro has green bract-like structures, a magenta protruding flowering tuft and photographer's 2-mm ruler. This view does NOT resolve 4–12 subtending bristles or the short knotty rhizome. Do not label magenta floral parts as sterile bristles.
items.why_it_matters: KNOTROOT BRISTLEGRASS (perennial): FIRST verify a living short hard knotty basal rhizome, then a generally short even-width dense foxtail head (~3–8 cm). FNA reports 4–12 persistent bristles, 2–12 mm long, beneath each spikelet; they must be counted from a genuinely intact head at 10–20×. Our only stored macro shows green bracts and pink emergent floral tissue with a 2-mm scale, NOT the perennial rhizome or a countable group of 4–12 basal bristles.

items.label: Southwestern bristlegrass — long projecting bristles
items.image_role: Existing exact-source flowering photograph: conspicuous long bristles and spikelet-bearing axis visible
items.caption: Kyla Miller's source photo clearly shows a long tapered green flowering axis, many ovoid pale spikelets and conspicuously long, outward-pointing bristles. The photo does not itself prove each bristle belongs to just one spikelet or provide a measurement ruler.
items.why_it_matters: SOUTHWESTERN / SCHEELE'S BRISTLEGRASS (perennial): a tall, commonly broad-leaved and hairy grass with a long, tapered, rather open bottlebrush-like head. Usually 1 (sometimes 2–3) LONG separate projecting bristles per spikelet, typically 10–35 mm in FNA/Kew. Unlike Reverchon's shorter sparse bristles, these long bristles are actually obvious in the saved flowering photograph. Edwards Plateau shady limestone canyon habitat is supportive, not conclusive.
